extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, respondents and counsel in USPTO disciplinary proceedings (OED and accused practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural rules, evidence burdens, trust-account and fee-division requirements, and sanctioning factors applied in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) disciplinary proceedings. Covers summary judgment practice, pleading requirements, and substantive professional-conduct rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence. Thereafter, Respondent has the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clear and convincing standard is intermediate between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt; it requires evidence “of such weight that it produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, as to the truth of the allegations.” (citing Addington, Jimenez, Foster). Use this standard when assessing sufficiency of proof in OED disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard in USPTO disciplinary cases (37 C.F.R. § 11.43; Fed. R. Civ. P. 56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions commonly filed under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, including motions for summary judgment, may be filed in USPTO disciplinary cases. The Court applies the Rule 56(c) standard: summary judgment is appropriate where there is a lack of a genuine, triable issue of material fact and under governing law there can be but one reasonable conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An issue is genuine only if a reasonable factfinder could rule for either party; a fact is material if it could affect the outcome under governing law (Anderson, Celotex). Nonmoving parties must point to specific facts or evidence creating a triable issue; mere allegations or denials are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading requirements — specific admissions/denials and timely defenses (37 C.F.R. § 11.36)
rubrics_metrics.description: In answering a complaint, a respondent must specifically admit or deny each allegation and must specify all defenses, their nexus to the misconduct, and the reason each provides a defense or mitigation. Any defenses not timely raised in an answer cannot be relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every allegation not denied is deemed admitted and may be considered proven (11.36(d)). Untimely assertions of affirmative defenses are prejudicial and may be stricken; leave to amend must be sought prior to discovery closure to avoid prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery authorization (37 C.F.R. § 11.52)
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent does not have an automatic right to conduct discovery; discovery must be authorized by the Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties seeking discovery in USPTO disciplinary proceedings must move for and obtain leave of the Court under 37 C.F.R. § 11.52. Failure to request or obtain leave may preclude use of discovery to oppose summary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing a sanction, the Court must consider: (1) Whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these four factors (and consult ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for aggravating/mitigating context) when choosing an appropriate sanction (suspension, exclusion, reprimand, etc.). Consider actual vs. potential injury and weigh aggravators such as prior disciplinary history, pattern, multiple violations, refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing, and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for suspended/excluded practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded or suspended practitioner may act as a paralegal or perform services normally performed by laypersons for another practitioner only if (i) the excluded/suspended practitioner is a salaried employee of the other practitioner or firm, or employs the other practitioner as a salaried employee; and (ii) the excluded/suspended practitioner is under the supervision of the other practitioner who assumes full, professional responsibility to clients and the Office for work performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the above conditions are met, the excluded/suspended practitioner is expressly prohibited from: communicating directly with the other practitioner's clients regarding any immediate or prospective business before the Office, and from rendering legal advice or legal services to those clients regarding business before the Office. Independent-contractor arrangements and direct client communications by excluded practitioners violate 11.58(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safekeeping of client funds (37 C.F.R. § 11.115)
rubrics_metrics.description: Client funds must be kept separate from practitioner funds. If funds involve legal fees or expenses paid in advance, they must be deposited into a client trust account and only drawn on when fees are earned and expenses incurred. Absent client consent, client funds must be kept in an account maintained in the state where the practitioner’s office is situated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must not deposit client advances into personal accounts or accounts in another state (e.g., depositing client funds into an account in Hawaii when principal office is in New York violates 11.115(a)). Ensure withdrawals are proper, funds are only disbursed for named payees, and signatory authority is limited to the practitioner or persons under direct supervision (11.115(f)(2)(i)-(iii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required trust account records (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must maintain specified records for accounts holding client funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required records include: (a) receipt and disbursement journals recording deposits and withdrawals with date, source, and description and payee/purpose; (b) ledger records for each client showing source/amounts/charges/disbursements; (c) copies of retainer and compensation agreements; (d) copies of accountings to clients/third persons; (e) copies of bills for fees/expenses rendered; (f) copies of records showing disbursements on behalf of clients; (g) equivalents of checkbook registers, bank statements, pre-numbered canceled checks, substitute checks; (h) records of all electronic transfers including authorizer, date, recipient, account number and confirmation; (i) monthly trial balances and quarterly reconciliations; (j) copies of client-file portions reasonably related to trust transactions. Failure to maintain these records violates 11.115.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on commingling client funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not commingle client funds with their own personal funds or non-client funds in the same account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositing client funds into an account that also contains practitioner or family personal funds (or an account owned/controlled by the practitioner's spouse) is prohibited. Such commingling creates potential for loss and subject-to-attachment risk and supports severe sanctioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawals and signatory safeguards for client accounts (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(2)(i)-(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must ensure that only the practitioner or a person under the practitioner's direct supervision has signatory authority on client trust accounts, and that withdrawals are made only by check payable to a named payee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks payable to vague payees (e.g., 'Petty Cash') or allowing non-authorized persons to sign are violations. Electronic transfers must be documented with authorizer and recipient information. Maintain monthly reconciliations and controls to prevent misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on impermissible division of fees (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing legal fees with another practitioner in an impermissible manner (e.g., without proper client consent/documentation) violates USPTO rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee-sharing arrangements should be disclosed to clients and comply with applicable rules (the decision noted that Respondent collected fees and paid the other practitioner directly, and neither counseled clients about the fee division nor obtained clients’ written consent). Failure to obtain client consent or to document fee division supports a finding of impermissible fee division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence rules — hearsay and admissibility in disciplinary hearings (37 C.F.R. § 11.50(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of evidence prevailing in courts of law and equity are not controlling in disciplinary hearings; the proceedings are governed by the regulations and the clear and convincing standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearsay may be considered if it meets the clear-and-convincing threshold; however, absence of direct evidence or failure to rebut admitted allegations can result in summary judgment where nonmoving party does not produce evidence in opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective prosecution defense standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail on selective prosecution, a respondent must show (1) he was singled out while similarly situated violators were not pursued, and (2) the OED Director pursued action invidiously or in bad faith (based on impermissible considerations such as race, religion, or to prevent exercise of constitutional rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of mere selectivity, without proof of invidious or bad-faith motivation, cannot sustain a selective-prosecution claim (citing Smithfield, Hendrickson). The nonmoving party must produce specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and prejudice in asserting defenses and motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmative defenses or special matters not pleaded in the answer are generally barred; untimely assertion is prejudicial and will usually be disallowed unless leave is granted and opposition has opportunity to develop a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek leave to amend early (before discovery closes); courts apply prejudice analysis and may strike late-defenses (citing Thomas v. FTS USA). Raising defenses for the first time on the eve of hearing or on summary judgment is untimely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of competency and familiarity with USPTO rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners owe duties to clients to serve competently, which includes maintaining familiarity with USPTO rules (including disciplinary rules) governing practitioner conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner's extensive experience is an aggravating factor; ignorance of the Office's rules is not an acceptable defense where orders and regulations clearly prohibit the conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to respond or pursue discovery at summary judgment (Celotex principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a respondent fails to investigate allegations, obtain discovery, or point to evidence raising a genuine issue of material fact, allegations not specifically denied or supported may be deemed admitted and summary judgment appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonmoving parties cannot be 'lax' in pursuing discovery; courts may treat non-denials as admissions and accept the moving party's material facts when the respondent does not present contrary specific evidence.
